sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
GORM is a Go ORM that maps structs and model relationships to database operations. It provides query builders, conventions, associations, hooks, and migration helpers on top of a SQL database driver.

A `*gorm.DB` builds statements through chained methods and scans results into structs. Zero values, selected fields, association loading, transaction handles, and error values affect the generated SQL, so developers still need to inspect what runs.

For example, `db.WithContext(ctx).Where("email = ?", email).First(&user)` binds the email as a value and returns `gorm.ErrRecordNotFound` when no record matches. Debug or dry-run logging can show the generated statement.

An ORM does not remove the need to understand SQL, indexes, transactions, constraints, connection pools, and query plans. Production schema changes may need versioned migration tools and review beyond GORM's automatic migration helper.

GORM is useful for routine CRUD and relationship-heavy application code where its conventions reduce repeated mapping. Direct SQL remains valuable for complex reports, database-specific features, carefully tuned queries, or teams that want every statement explicit.

sections.title: The core model: GORM in a Go service
sections.content:
GORM in a Go service is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

An ORM changes the level at which application code expresses database work, but it does not change what the database executes. GORM reads model metadata and chained query options, produces SQL, sends values through a driver, and maps returned columns back into fields. That convenience is strongest for standard create, read, update, and delete flows. It becomes less helpful when the query is the important design artifact, such as a complex aggregate or database-specific operation. Model behaviour also has rules worth testing: updates may skip zero values depending on the API used, associations can be loaded lazily through extra application calls, and missing records have a distinct error. Transactions must use the transaction-scoped handle just as `database/sql` code uses `*sql.Tx`. A healthy GORM codebase therefore keeps query logging or tracing available, watches statement counts, uses database constraints, and permits direct SQL where it is clearer.

sections.title: GORM in a Go service example
sections.content:
~~~go
var user User
result := db.WithContext(ctx).
    Preload("Roles").
    Where("email = ?", email).
    First(&user)

if errors.Is(result.Error, gorm.ErrRecordNotFound) {
    return User{}, ErrUserNotFound
}
return user, result.Error
~~~

sections.title: GORM in a Go service at a glance
sections.content:
| Need | GORM | Direct SQL |
|---|---|---|
| Routine model CRUD | Less mapping code | More explicit code |
| Exact complex query | Possible, but abstraction may add noise | Query is fully visible |
| Relationships | Association helpers and preload | Explicit joins or several queries |
| Database knowledge | Still required | Required directly |
